B) Returning to the coast as an adult visitor
C) The experience of its absence after moving away
D) Being told by others how special it was

examples.passage: The old librarian knew every book in the building, not by title, but by the quality of the silence each one created in the room when it was being read. Some books left a tense silence, as if their readers were holding their breath. Others left a soft, drifting silence that seemed to settle into the wood of the tables themselves.

question.question: What does the librarian's unusual way of knowing the books most suggest about her relationship to the library?
options: A) She has read every single book in the library and remembers each one in detail
B) She has spent so much time observing readers that the books are known to her through their effects on others
C) She believes that books are best understood by examining their physical bindings closely
D) She is unable to read the books herself and so must judge them only by their covers

53.description: B1. Month 16. Clear exposition with examples. Some technical vocabulary used precisely. Vocabulary around 4,600 words.

examples.passage: Memory does not work like a recording. Each time we remember something, we reconstruct it slightly differently, influenced by what we have experienced since. This is why two people who witnessed the same event can describe it in completely different ways.

question.question: Why, according to the passage, might two witnesses give different accounts of the same event?
options: A) One of the two witnesses may simply not be telling the full truth
B) They were standing in different places and so saw different parts of the event
C) Each person's later experiences have quietly reshaped how they remember it
D) Memory works like a recording that gradually gets corrupted over time

examples.passage: A coral reef is not a single organism but an enormous community. Each coral animal is tiny, but together they build the limestone structures that house thousands of species of fish, plants, and other creatures. When the water grows too warm, the corals expel the algae that feed them and slowly starve. The reef does not die all at once; it fades, and the community fades with it.

question.question: What does the description of how a reef dies most clearly emphasize?
options: A) The collapse is sudden, beginning and ending in the same single moment of crisis
B) Warm water has no significant effect on the survival of corals over time
C) The death of the reef is gradual and pulls down a much wider system with it
D) Reefs can recover quickly because they are made up of so many different organisms

54.description: B1. Month 16–17. Comparative paragraph holding two or more cases in parallel. Vocabulary near 4,900 words.

examples.passage: In many cultures, sharing a meal is much more than just eating. It is a tradition that brings family members closer together and marks important events. The food itself is often less important than the meaning of eating together.

question.question: What does the writer identify as the main value of dining together?
options: A) The quality of the dishes is what makes such gatherings worthwhile
B) Such gatherings matter most during formal religious occasions
C) The human connection it creates carries more weight than what is served
D) They are mainly important for bonding with strangers

examples.passage: Throughout history, music has often crossed borders more easily than language. A song written in one country can move listeners on the other side of the world without translation. This may be because rhythm and melody speak to feelings that lie beneath the level of words — feelings that all human beings share but that no language ever fully captures.

question.question: Why does the writer suggest music crosses borders more easily than language?
options: A) Because most popular music today happens to be sung in widely understood languages
B) Because melody and rhythm reach a layer of feeling that words cannot fully express
C) Because translation is too difficult and slow to keep pace with international travel
D) Because feelings are felt in different ways by different cultures of the world

55.description: B1–B2 boundary. Month 17. Moderate complexity and fluency. Some idiomatic language and varied sentence structures. Vocabulary around 5,200 words. The writing feels natural and connected rather than constructed.

examples.passage: She had lived in the same apartment for twelve years, and by now it felt less like a home than a habit. Every morning she followed the same route to work, passed the same faces, bought coffee from the same cart. She told herself this was stability. On difficult days, she was not so sure.

question.question: What does the phrase 'felt less like a home than a habit' suggest about her situation?
options: A) Her apartment is uncomfortable and she wants to move out
B) She has confused routine with genuine contentment in her life
C) She values stability and is fully satisfied with how things are
D) Building habits is always a solid foundation for happiness

examples.passage: The painter worked outdoors in all weathers, even when the wind made the canvas shake on the easel. Friends thought he was being foolish; he insisted that a painting made indoors from memory was always thinner than one made in the presence of the thing itself. He was not interested, he said, in the look of a tree, but in the strange resistance the world offered when you tried to set it down.

question.question: What does the painter's stated reason for working outdoors most clearly reveal about his idea of art?
options: A) He believes painting is a form of careful documentation of every visible detail
B) He values direct contact with the subject because he is interested in struggle, not appearance
C) He prefers difficult conditions because they impress his friends and fellow painters
D) He thinks indoor painting is technically inferior because the light there is too steady

56.description: B1. About 18 months. Vocabulary roughly 5,500 words active. Varied sentence structures, clear argumentation, emerging idioms. Comparable in difficulty to a standard newspaper article or short popular nonfiction.

examples.passage: Researchers have long debated whether cities make people happier or more isolated. New data suggests the answer depends heavily on factors like income, age, and access to green space. Those who live near parks and community spaces report significantly higher levels of wellbeing, regardless of how densely populated their neighborhood is.

question.question: What does the finding about parks challenge in the ongoing debate about cities?
options: A) The idea that income has any effect on happiness
B) The assumption that population density alone decides urban wellbeing
C) The claim that cities always and automatically make people happier
D) The view that green space matters more than any community factor

examples.passage: For most of recorded history, mathematicians treated zero with deep suspicion. The very idea of a number representing nothing seemed contradictory, even dangerous to philosophical systems built on the principle that everything that exists must be something. The eventual acceptance of zero, brought to Europe through Indian and Arab scholarship, was not merely a technical advance. It was a quiet revolution in how the West allowed itself to think.

question.question: Why does the writer call the acceptance of zero 'a quiet revolution in how the West allowed itself to think'?
options: A) Because zero proved to be useful in advanced calculations across many areas of mathematics
B) Because accepting zero required the West to permit a concept its philosophy had previously ruled out
C) Because Indian and Arab scholars had already used zero for many centuries before its arrival
D) Because zero made it possible to write much larger numbers than had been written before

57.description: B1–B2. Month 18–20. Sustained argument with a thesis, evidence, and concluding observation. Vocabulary near 5,800 words.

examples.passage: The appeal of nostalgia is easy to understand but hard to justify. We tend to remember the past not as it was but as we wished it to be, editing out the discomforts and magnifying the warmth. Politicians who promise to restore a golden age are selling a version of history that never quite existed.

question.question: What is the passage implying about political promises to 'restore a golden age'?
options: A) Such promises work because voters remember the past accurately
B) Politicians understand history better than most ordinary people do
C) These promises exploit a tendency to remember the past as better than it was
D) Nostalgia is a reliable guide to deciding which past policies succeeded

examples.passage: Watching a great chess player is a peculiar experience. The board itself looks unchanged for long stretches; almost nothing happens. Yet to those who can read the position, an entire drama is unfolding — possibilities being weighed, threats being prepared, choices being silently abandoned. The spectacle is one of pure intellect, which is also why so few people can bear to sit through it.

question.question: What does the writer suggest about the appeal of watching chess?
options: A) It is enjoyable because the action on the board is constantly changing in visible ways
B) Most viewers can easily follow the underlying calculations of professional players
C) Its drama is real but invisible, which makes it inaccessible to most spectators
D) Chess is a poor spectator sport because nothing of any importance ever truly occurs

58.description: B1–B2. Month 20. Accessible exposition of complex ideas with concrete illustrations. Some figurative language. Vocabulary around 6,100 words.

examples.passage: The deep ocean is one of the least understood places on Earth. Below a thousand meters, sunlight disappears entirely and the water is near freezing. Yet life thrives there, in forms so unusual they seem to belong to another world — fish with their own built-in lights, creatures that can survive pressures that would crush a submarine.

question.question: The comparison to 'another world' is used to convey what about deep-sea life?
options: A) Deep-sea creatures may have come from outer space originally
B) The ocean floor is as little explored as other planets are
C) The creatures are so strange in form that they go beyond ordinary expectation
D) Scientists find studying the deep ocean more exciting than studying space

examples.passage: The ancient Greeks believed that the gods themselves had set the stars in their fixed positions, and that the small wandering points of light were planets — the word itself means 'wanderer.' For centuries, no one could explain why these few stars moved while the rest stayed still. The answer, when it finally came, would require giving up the comforting picture of an Earth at the center of everything.

question.question: What does the passage suggest the explanation of planetary motion required from human thinkers?
options: A) Better telescopes capable of clearly resolving the small wandering points of light
B) The acceptance of a worldview that displaced humanity from the cosmic center
C) A return to the original Greek belief that the gods had set every star in place
D) The recognition that the planets were not really moving across the sky after all

59.description: B2 approach. Month 21. Sentence variety increases; the prose has rhythm. Observation, reflection, and a small argumentative thread. Vocabulary near 6,400 words.

examples.passage: There is something particular about the quiet of a library — not the absence of sound exactly, but the active suppression of it, as if everyone present has agreed to a shared form of consideration. It is one of the few public spaces where silence is still taken seriously.

question.question: How does the author distinguish library quiet from ordinary silence?
options: A) Libraries are completely soundproofed, unlike other public buildings
B) The quiet in a library is passively present rather than actively kept up
C) It is a collectively upheld behavior, not simply the absence of noise
D) Libraries stay quiet because very few people visit them regularly

examples.passage: Long-distance running is often described as a sport, but it has always seemed to me more like a form of negotiation. The runner is not really competing with the others on the course; they are bargaining with their own body, asking it for one more kilometer in exchange for the brief illusion of being in control. The body usually agrees. Until, one day, it does not.

question.question: What does the writer's framing of running as 'negotiation' rather than 'sport' chiefly emphasize?
options: A) Running races are won through clever bargaining with one's competitors on the course
B) The real contest is internal, and the body's eventual refusal is part of its terms
C) Long-distance runners do not compete against each other in any meaningful sense
D) Control of one's body is fully attainable through proper training and preparation

60.description: B2 entry. Month 22. Reflective prose that moves toward an implicit thesis through accumulated observation. Vocabulary near 6,500 words.

examples.passage: There is a particular kind of attention required to walk in a city you do not yet know. You notice things — the angle at which a shop sign leans, the way the light falls on a doorway, an accent you cannot quite place — because nothing yet is filtered out by familiarity. The same street, walked daily for a year, becomes nearly invisible. The city does not change; you do. This is not a loss exactly, but it is something. The price of being at home in a place is forgetting how strange it once seemed.

question.question: What does the writer suggest happens as a place becomes familiar?
options: A) Cities present their best qualities only to long-term residents
B) Familiarity is what makes a place feel like home over time
C) Habit makes a familiar environment effectively invisible
D) Travelers see cities more accurately than people who live in them

examples.passage: Cooking from a recipe is a strangely social act, even when performed alone. The recipe is the trace of someone else's experiment, refined through repetition and eventually written down. To follow it is to step briefly into their kitchen, their assumptions about what a pan should sound like at a given heat, what 'a pinch' means in their hands. Even improvisation, when it happens, happens against the background of inherited technique. We praise originality in cooks, but most of what looks like originality is a long conversation with the dead, conducted in stock and salt.

question.question: What does the writer mean by calling cooking from a recipe 'strangely social'?
options: A) Recipes are typically shared at gatherings of friends and family
B) The cook is following instructions shaped by another person's prior experience
C) Cooking together is more rewarding than cooking alone in the kitchen
D) Modern recipes encourage cooks to share photos of their results online

61.description: B2 approach. Month 22. Abstract nouns and more formal register emerge. Confident, varied prose. Vocabulary around 6,700 words.

examples.passage: The relationship between language and thought is more intimate than we usually acknowledge. The words available to us in any given moment shape not only how we communicate but what we are able to conceive. Cultures that lack a word for a specific emotion do not simply lack a term — they may lack the concept itself.

question.question: What is the strongest claim the passage makes about the role of language?
options: A) Language is mainly a tool for expressing ideas that already exist in the mind
B) Lacking a word for something simply means speakers avoid discussing that topic
C) Language can set the very limits of what people are capable of thinking at all
D) Emotions are shaped by culture but can still be described in any language

examples.passage: It has become fashionable to praise failure as a stepping-stone to success, as if every setback were a hidden gift. The reality is less convenient. Most failures teach nothing; they merely cost time, money, and the slow erosion of confidence. The few that do teach are those one is willing to examine without self-flattery — which is rare, because the most useful lessons are also the most painful.

question.question: What is the writer's central argument about the popular celebration of failure?
options: A) Failure should be celebrated more enthusiastically than it currently is in modern culture
B) Most failures are valuable because they always lead to a kind of personal growth
C) Failure becomes useful only through unflattering self-examination, which most people avoid
D) Setbacks should be hidden because their effects on confidence are too damaging

62.description: B2. About 2 years. Vocabulary roughly 7,000–8,000 words. Sustained argumentation, figurative language, subordinate clauses, and moderate stylistic complexity. Comparable in difficulty to a quality newspaper feature or accessible popular nonfiction.

examples.passage: Democracy depends not only on institutions but on habits of mind that no constitution can mandate. Citizens must be willing to extend some basic trust to people whose views they find repugnant, to accept election results they find bitterly disappointing, and to believe that disagreement can be legitimate without being treasonous. When those habits erode, laws alone are rarely sufficient to restore them.

question.question: What does the author suggest is the fundamental limitation of legal and institutional safeguards for democracy?
options: A) Constitutions are too rigid to respond to changing political conditions over time
B) Laws cannot produce the psychological habits democracy needs in order to function
C) Citizens in modern democracies lack the education to understand their legal rights
D) Democratic institutions only remain stable when backed by the threat of force

examples.passage: The history of medicine is, in part, a history of confident error. Bloodletting, lobotomy, the routine prescription of mercury — each was, in its time, defended by the leading authorities of the day, supported by what was understood as evidence, and resisted only by a few who were dismissed as cranks. The lesson is not that the experts of every era are wrong. It is that the practices we currently take for granted will, in time, be revisited with the same uneasy curiosity we now turn on the practices of the past.

question.question: What is the writer's central point about contemporary medical practice?
options: A) Today's doctors should categorically reject the medical practices of past centuries as foolish
B) Modern medicine has finally escaped the kind of confident error that plagued earlier eras
C) Our present certainties will likely be reassessed in the same way we now reassess past ones
D) The dissenting cranks of every era turn out to have been correct in nearly every case

63.description: B2. 2 years. Longer sentences balanced against short ones for effect. A clear authorial voice begins to emerge. Vocabulary near 8,500 words.

examples.passage: There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes not from being alone but from being surrounded by people with whom you have nothing in common. It is the loneliness of a party you cannot leave, of a conversation that never quite touches anything real. Some people spend years trying to explain it; others simply learn to carry it.

question.question: What does the image of 'a party you cannot leave' contribute to the passage's argument?
options: A) It suggests that social obligations make this loneliness sharper than simple solitude
B) It implies that parties are by their nature always superficial and hollow events
C) It shows that physical closeness to others has nothing to do with feeling lonely
D) It reveals that the speaker dislikes social gatherings of any kind

examples.passage: What rivers carry, in addition to water, is time. The pebbles at the bottom were once jagged stones, and before that they were part of cliffs that no longer exist. The river itself does not remember any of this; it simply continues. Standing beside it, one is reminded that patience and force can amount to the same thing if you give them long enough.

question.question: What does the writer ultimately want the reader to take from the river's example?
options: A) Cliffs are surprisingly fragile and tend to collapse much more quickly than people realize
B) The distinction between gentle persistence and overwhelming force can dissolve over enough time
C) Rivers should be admired chiefly for their visible strength rather than their gradual effects
D) Patience is a moral virtue that nature happens to model better than human beings ever do

64.description: B2. 2–2.5 years. Sensory detail, metaphor, and reflection integrated into the prose. Vocabulary around 9,000 words.

examples.passage: My grandfather's house smelled of sawdust and tobacco long after he had stopped working wood and given up smoking. Memory, I think, is largely a matter of smell — not images or voices but the physical trace of time, caught in objects and rooms long after the moment has passed.

question.question: What does the detail about the smells persisting after the grandfather stopped those activities illustrate about memory?
options: A) Smell is a stronger trigger of memory than sight or sound ever is
B) The physical world holds traces of the past even when the actions behind them are gone
C) Memory works most reliably when we are near familiar smells and objects
D) The grandfather's house was simply not well ventilated over the years

examples.passage: The democracies of the world have grown remarkably skilled at producing the appearance of accountability — committees, inquiries, hearings, reports — without producing the substance. The reports are written, filed, and quoted, and life continues exactly as it did before. One begins to suspect that the rituals of accountability have become, for many institutions, the most reliable way of avoiding it.

question.question: What is the central irony the writer identifies in modern democratic accountability?
options: A) Inquiries fail because the public has lost interest in the reports those inquiries finally produce
B) The visible mechanisms of accountability now function as a substitute for the thing they pretend to enact
C) Hearings would work much better if they were held in private rather than in any public setting
D) Accountability has become impossible because modern institutions have grown too large for it

65.description: B2. 2.5 years. Longer analytical argument with counterarguments acknowledged. Concessive and conditional structures used skillfully. Vocabulary near 9,500 words.

examples.passage: It is tempting to argue that technology has shortened our attention spans. The evidence, however, is more ambiguous than the claim suggests. People concentrate deeply on video games, long films, and serialized fiction for hours at a time. What has changed is not the capacity for attention but the environment that competes for it.

question.question: What distinction does the author draw that complicates the 'shrinking attention spans' narrative?
options: A) Attention spans vary so much by age group that the claim is too general to defend
B) The ability to focus has not declined; what has grown is the number of things competing for it
C) Video games and long films are not demanding enough to count as real sustained attention
D) Technology has actually improved attention spans for certain kinds of demanding content

examples.passage: Critics of museums often describe them as warehouses for stolen goods, and there is some truth in the charge. Yet to dismiss the modern museum entirely is to forget what it has also become: a public space where strangers stand together before objects they could not otherwise encounter, and in doing so participate, however briefly, in a culture not their own. Whether such participation can ever fully repay the original taking is a question that may admit no clean answer.

question.question: What does the writer's closing question signal about their stance on museums?
options: A) They believe the modern museum has fully made amends for the historical wrongs of acquisition
B) They reject the criticism of museums as colonial warehouses entirely and without qualification
C) They acknowledge real value in museums while refusing to pretend the moral problem is settled
D) They argue that the original taking is irrelevant because the public benefit is so significant

66.description: B2. 2.5–3 years. Polished prose with controlled emotion, specific detail, and observation. Vocabulary around 10,000 words.

examples.passage: She learned the language in fragments — a word here, a phrase there — the way you might reassemble a broken plate, knowing that the cracks will always show. But she also learned that a plate with cracks can still hold water, still be beautiful in its way, and still be used every day without apology.

question.question: What does the cracked plate metaphor ultimately argue about imperfect language learning?
options: A) An imperfect learner should apologize for the errors they make in speech
B) Incomplete learning makes a language both less useful and less beautiful to hear
C) Signs of effort and incompleteness do not stop a language from being functional and even beautiful
D) Language learning should always start with complete phrases rather than single words

examples.passage: The desert at dawn does not so much fill with light as relinquish its darkness, grudgingly, color by color. The first hint is a thinning of the black above the eastern ridge; then a band of slate; then a softer grey, and finally — almost as a surprise, though one has been waiting for it — the violent orange that announces the sun. By midmorning the sky will have forgotten this entire small ceremony, and so, mostly, will the watcher.

question.question: What does the description of dawn 'relinquishing' its darkness rather than 'filling with light' chiefly convey?
options: A) The writer prefers night to day and wishes the darkness would last considerably longer than it does
B) The change is unwilling and incremental — what arrives is felt as a slow yielding rather than an arrival
C) Light is illusory and never actually appears in the desert at all in any genuine and observable sense
D) The desert is a much darker landscape than other places when the sun has finished rising over it

67.description: B2. 3 years. Rich vocabulary, metaphor, and syntactic variety used purposefully. Vocabulary roughly 10,000–12,000 words. Comparable in difficulty to a quality literary novel for general adult readers or a long-form magazine essay.

examples.passage: The city changes so fast that nostalgia is almost a reflex here — people mourn neighborhoods that disappeared a decade ago, and mourn the mourning itself as a kind of sentimentality. There is a version of every city that exists only in the memory of those who knew it at a particular moment, and that version is, in its way, as real as any other.

question.question: What is the author suggesting when they say people 'mourn the mourning itself as a kind of sentimentality'?
options: A) People feel guilty for grieving changes that were entirely outside their control
B) Nostalgia has become self-aware — people notice and question their own longing for the past
C) Mourning a lost neighborhood is always a straightforward act of genuine feeling
D) People in this city are far more emotional than those who live in other cities

examples.passage: Athletes at the highest level rarely speak about their own talent. They speak about training, about preparation, about the dull accumulation of hours that no one ever sees. The reason, I have come to think, is not modesty. It is that talent at that level is so widely distributed it has almost stopped being a useful explanation; what distinguishes one champion from another is the part of the work that is least photogenic and least romantic — and, perhaps for that reason, the most reliable.

question.question: What is the writer's central explanation for why elite athletes downplay talent?
options: A) They have been trained by their coaches and publicists to project a humble image to the public
B) At their level talent is so widespread that the decisive factor is unseen, unglamorous work
C) Talent is in fact the only real explanation, but elite athletes are too modest to acknowledge it
D) They believe that explaining their success in terms of work will inspire other young athletes

68.description: B2–C1 boundary. 3–3.5 years. The prose handles abstraction and ambiguity with ease. Subtext operates beneath the surface. Vocabulary near 12,000 words.

examples.passage: What we call common sense is usually nothing more than the unexamined assumptions of our particular time and place dressed up in the language of inevitability. Every era believes its prejudices to be observations. It takes unusual courage — or unusual distance — to see the difference.

question.question: Why does the author present 'courage' and 'distance' as alternative routes to the same insight?
options: A) Courage means ignoring common sense, while distance means moving to a new place
B) One must either actively resist the assumptions of one's era or be removed from them to see their contingency
C) Courage is what it takes to accept common sense, while distance lends perspective on it
D) Both words describe the same emotional state that follows an intellectual discovery

examples.passage: Mountains are, in some sense, our most honest landscapes. They do not pretend to be useful. They cannot be cultivated, persuaded, or hurried. What they offer is a glimpse of duration in a form that humbles ordinary timescales: ranges that were rising while our species was still arboreal, summits that will be ground down to nothing while our descendants, if any, are doing things we could not now imagine. The proper response, I have always thought, is not awe so much as a kind of quiet relief.

question.question: What unusual emotional response to mountains does the writer endorse, and why?
options: A) Awe, because mountains stand as a vivid demonstration of nature's overwhelming and decorative power
B) Relief, because the geological scale of mountains liberates the observer from the inflation of human concerns
C) Disappointment, because mountains turn out to be useful and persuadable in ways the writer dislikes
D) Indifference, because mountains have no relevant relationship to the lives of ordinary modern people

69.description: B2–C1. 3.5 years. Modal hedging ('it seems,' 'in some sense,' 'one might say') marks uncertainty without abandoning argument. Vocabulary around 12,200 words.

examples.passage: It is tempting to read history as a series of moral lessons, but the lessons are rarely as legible as we would like. The same events, viewed at different distances, suggest different conclusions, and even contemporaries disagreed sharply about what they were witnessing. To insist on a single moral reading is, in some sense, to flatten the texture of the past — to mistake the cleanness of a story for the truth of an event. The temptation is understandable; complexity is uncomfortable, and a tidy lesson lets us close the book and move on. But the historians worth reading rarely let us.

question.question: What does the writer warn against?
options: A) Drawing any moral conclusions whatsoever from historical events
B) Reducing the complexity of past events to a single tidy lesson
C) Allowing contemporary observers to dictate how history is read today
D) The growing tendency among historians to disagree with one another

examples.passage: Most diaries are not, in any honest sense, written for the self. The diarist is keenly aware, however much they protest otherwise, that words on paper persist in a way that thought does not — that someone, eventually, may read them. This awareness shapes the writing in ways the diarist may not fully recognise: a tendency to compose rather than confess, to leave out what would embarrass, to elevate ordinary days into something worth recording. The result is not a faithful record but a portrait already in negotiation with a future audience, even when that audience is imagined as no one in particular.

question.question: What does the writer claim about diary-writing?
options: A) Most diarists secretly intend their work to be published after their death
B) The presence of an imagined future reader subtly shapes what gets written
C) Honest diary-writing requires the writer to abandon all literary instincts
D) Most diaries lose their value once the diarist is no longer alive

70.description: B2–C1. 3.5 years. Layered meaning and sophisticated sentence construction. Complex nominal phrases, embedded relative clauses. Vocabulary around 12,500 words.

examples.passage: The novel, at its best, is a machine for generating empathy — a device that places the reader inside a consciousness not their own and asks them to inhabit it long enough to feel its logic. This is not escapism. It is, in fact, one of the more serious things a person can do with their time.

question.question: How does the author use the word 'escapism' strategically in this passage?
options: A) To admit that reading novels is pleasant but ultimately without real value
B) To name and dismiss a common objection before asserting the opposite position
C) To argue that all escapism is worthwhile so long as it produces empathy in readers
D) To draw a clear line between serious literary novels and lighter genre fiction

examples.passage: When chemists isolated the element polonium, they named it for the homeland of the woman who had discovered it — a country that, at that moment, did not exist on any official map. The naming was, in this sense, doubly defiant: it asserted both a scientific priority and a national one, the former in the language of the laboratory, the latter in the silent register of acts that refuse to be merely scientific.

question.question: What does the writer mean by calling the act of naming 'doubly defiant'?
options: A) The chemists defied scientific convention by naming an element after a person rather than a property
B) The naming made one claim openly within science and a second, unspoken claim about national existence
C) The chemists deliberately defied the political authorities of every country involved in the discovery
D) The act of naming was illegal under the laws of two separate nations at the time it occurred

71.description: C1 approach. 4 years. Argument unfolds across multiple sentences with qualifications, concessions, and precise distinctions. Vocabulary near 13,000 words.

examples.passage: To speak of a culture's values as if they were a coherent system is to import a kind of order that rarely exists in practice. Values conflict, overlap, and contradict one another in ways that anthropologists have documented repeatedly. What holds a society together is not agreement but a shared tolerance for disagreement within certain limits — limits that are themselves contested.

question.question: What does the phrase 'limits that are themselves contested' add to the author's argument about social cohesion?
options: A) It undermines the whole argument by implying that no society can hold together at all
B) It refines the argument by noting that even the boundaries of acceptable disagreement are disputed
C) It suggests that the most fundamental values in any society are always agreed upon by everyone
D) It implies that social scientists are unable to study cultural values in an objective way

examples.passage: It is sometimes said that beauty in mathematics is a sentimental fiction — that the term 'elegant proof' is no more than a flattering name for 'short proof.' But mathematicians who use the word do not seem to mean brevity. They mean something closer to inevitability: a sense that the result, having been seen, could not have arrived in any other way. That this experience occurs reliably across very different minds suggests it is tracking something real about the structure of the demonstration, even if the something has so far resisted definition.

question.question: How does the writer position the dismissal of mathematical beauty as merely sentimental?
options: A) They concede it fully and propose that mathematicians should stop using the word 'elegant'
B) They reject it on the grounds that the cross-mind reliability of the experience suggests it tracks something genuine
C) They neither endorse nor reject it but recommend further empirical investigation by mathematicians
D) They argue that elegance is a private experience that cannot be reliably communicated between people

72.description: C1 approach. 4–4.5 years. Complex interior monologue or free indirect discourse. The prose rewards close attention. Vocabulary around 13,500 words.

examples.passage: He had the curious sensation, not unfamiliar to him, of watching himself from a slight distance — as though some calmer version of himself had stepped back to observe the proceedings with the mild interest of a stranger. He knew the feeling would pass. He also knew, from experience, that knowing this did not make it pass any faster.

question.question: What does the character's final observation — that knowing a feeling will pass does not accelerate its passing — reveal about his self-understanding?
options: A) He has lost the ability to regulate or manage his own emotions
B) He has genuine self-knowledge but sees its limits as a practical resource
C) He believes intellectual insight will eventually bring his emotional states under control
D) He has decided to stop attempting to understand his inner life altogether

examples.passage: The conductor lowered his baton without permitting the orchestra to come to its expected close, and for a moment the entire hall hung in the suspended silence of a sentence that has been broken off mid-clause. The audience did not, at first, applaud; they were not certain whether the piece was finished or merely interrupted, and the uncertainty itself, more than the music that preceded it, was what they would later remember as the most truthful part of the evening.

question.question: What does the audience's later judgment about the most 'truthful' part of the evening most clearly suggest?
options: A) The orchestra had played the piece so badly that its abrupt ending was a welcome and merciful relief
B) An experience of unresolved ambiguity can disclose something more honest than a polished performance does
C) The audience preferred the silence to the music itself because they were unfamiliar with the composer's style
D) The conductor had made an obvious mistake that the audience charitably interpreted as a deliberate artistic choice

73.description: C1. About 5 years. Vocabulary roughly 14,000–16,000 words. Complex syntax, nuanced register, embedded irony, sustained argument across multi-sentence units. Inferential reading required; not everything stated. Comparable in difficulty to literary fiction or long-form essays of the calibre of Orwell.

examples.passage: What strikes the reader of eighteenth-century moral philosophy is not how alien its concerns are but how persistent. The questions Hume and Smith were asking about sympathy, self-interest, and the nature of justice have not been answered — they have simply been translated into different vocabularies and distributed across different academic departments. The urgency, if anything, has increased.

question.question: What is the author implying when they say the questions have been 'translated into different vocabularies and distributed across different academic departments'?
options: A) Hume and Smith's philosophy has been conclusively resolved by modern social science
B) Academic specialization has split what were unified moral questions without actually settling them
C) Modern scholars have improved on eighteenth-century philosophy by using more precise language
D) Justice and sympathy are now studied more rigorously because multiple disciplines examine them

examples.passage: The Antarctic ice sheet, considered for most of the twentieth century to be a stable feature of the planetary system, is now understood to be governed by feedbacks whose past behavior provides only a partial guide to their future. Once a glacier retreats past certain bedrock thresholds, the geometry of the ice shelf can produce accelerating loss without any further forcing. What this means, practically, is that the slow rates of change observed today may bear little relation to the rates that follow once those thresholds are crossed.

question.question: What is the most important implication the writer draws from the bedrock-threshold dynamics?
options: A) Current observations are reassuring because the slow pace they show will continue indefinitely
B) Past stability of the ice sheet provides scientists with a clear model of its future behavior
C) Present rates of loss may be a poor guide to what happens once certain critical points are passed
D) Once a glacier retreats, the geometry stabilizes and further rapid loss is no longer expected

74.description: C1. 5–5.5 years. Long, carefully weighted sentences. Irony, moral complexity, and precise observation. Vocabulary near 16,000 words.

examples.passage: She was a woman who had spent so much of her life being competent that she had lost track of whether she was also happy. Competence had its own satisfactions, she supposed — the small, clean pleasure of a task completed, a problem solved, a situation managed — but she had begun to suspect that she had mistaken those satisfactions for something larger.

question.question: What is the precise nature of the error the character suspects she has made?
options: A) She chased competence at the direct cost of forming close personal relationships
B) She confused the narrow satisfactions of doing things well with a deeper form of fulfillment
C) She worked so hard for so long that she damaged her own physical health
D) She consistently underestimated her own level of competence throughout her life

examples.passage: He had always considered himself a man without illusions, which was, of course, the most flattering illusion of all. The discovery, when it came, did not arrive in the form of a single revelation but as a slow accretion of small embarrassments — the moments when his clear-eyed assessments of others turned out, on inspection, to be remarkably congenial to his own interests, and the moments when his refusal to flatter himself proved to be a more sophisticated kind of flattery still.

question.question: What is the structural irony the passage develops about the character's self-image?
options: A) His refusal to entertain illusions was itself the illusion that protected him from honest self-knowledge
B) He genuinely was a man without illusions, but came incorrectly to believe that he was not
C) His sophistication freed him from the kinds of small embarrassments that trouble less reflective people
D) Other people had been deceiving him about his own character for many years before the discovery

75.description: C1. 5.5 years. Technical vocabulary used precisely. Argument builds on previous paragraphs in a chain of reasoning. Vocabulary around 16,500 words.

examples.passage: The distinction between performative and constative utterances, which Austin introduced with characteristic tentativeness, was meant to mark a clean boundary between saying and doing. Subsequent philosophers of language have argued, with considerable force, that virtually any speech act can be understood as performing something, and that the notion of a purely descriptive utterance may be a theoretical fiction.

question.question: What happened to Austin's distinction between performative and constative utterances in subsequent philosophical debate?
options: A) It was universally accepted and refined into a precise and stable analytical tool
B) The boundary he drew was challenged by arguments that all speech acts have a performative dimension
C) It was rejected because Austin had presented his ideas with too little confidence initially
D) Philosophers agreed that constative utterances occur far more commonly than performative ones

examples.passage: Recent work in evolutionary biology has complicated the once-popular gene-centric account of inheritance. Epigenetic markers, microbiome composition, and even certain learned behaviors transmitted through parental care can produce trait variation across generations without any change in DNA sequence. None of this overturns the centrality of the gene, but it does suggest that the unit of selection is rather less clean a thing than the textbook diagrams have led several generations of undergraduates to assume.

question.question: What is the precise position the writer takes on the gene-centric view of inheritance?
options: A) Recent findings have completely overturned the gene-centric view, which now ought to be wholly abandoned
B) The gene retains its central role, but the boundary of what counts as the unit of selection has become blurred
C) Epigenetics, microbiome, and parental care fully replace genetic inheritance as the basis of trait variation
D) The textbook diagrams accurately describe inheritance and the recent findings have been substantially overstated

76.description: C1. 6 years. Allusions operate without signposting; a well-read audience is assumed. Vocabulary near 17,000 words.

examples.passage: Chekhov's great achievement was to make nothing happen in a way that felt like everything. His plots refuse the conventional satisfactions of resolution, preferring instead the off-key chord, the unfinished gesture, the silence where speech might have been. Readers who want events are perpetually disappointed; readers who want truth rarely are.

question.question: What does the contrast between the two types of readers imply about Chekhov's understanding of truth?
options: A) Truth in fiction is best conveyed through dramatic and decisive plot events
B) Truth lives in what is left unresolved or unspoken rather than in conclusive action
C) Only highly educated readers have the capacity to appreciate genuinely great literature
D) Chekhov intended for readers to feel let down by their expectations of his work

examples.passage: What separates the major composers of the late Romantic period from their lesser contemporaries is rarely a matter of technical equipment, which most of them possessed in abundance. It is, more often, a willingness to let the architecture of a work be deformed by the pressure of feeling — to allow the sonata form, when the music demands it, to bulge and crack, where the lesser composer would have smoothed the disturbance into the orderly cadence the inherited form recommends. The masterpieces are nearly always the works that bear the visible marks of this struggle.

question.question: What does the writer identify as the distinguishing mark of the major late Romantic composers?
options: A) A superior command of technique that allowed them to keep the inherited forms perfectly intact
B) A willingness to let emotional pressure visibly deform the inherited formal structures of the work
C) A preference for unfamiliar musical forms over the established sonata structures of their predecessors
D) An unusual ability to smooth disturbances into orderly cadences without disrupting the inherited form

77.description: C1–C2 boundary. 6–7 years. Considerable intellectual and stylistic density. Abstract ideas handled with precision and elegance. Vocabulary around 17,500 words.

examples.passage: The fear of death is not a simple thing. It is compounded of several distinct anxieties — the fear of pain, of loss, of non-existence, of irrelevance — and these are not always distinguishable from one another in the moment of experiencing them. Philosophy has tried, repeatedly and without complete success, to disentangle them, perhaps because they resist disentangling.

question.question: What does the author suggest about philosophy's project of analyzing the fear of death?
options: A) Philosophy has fully succeeded in separating each distinct anxiety involved in it
B) The fear of death is too simple a topic to benefit from philosophical examination
C) These anxieties may resist neat separation because of how they are lived from the inside
D) Philosophy ought to give up on this question entirely since it remains unanswerable

examples.passage: There is a peculiar pleasure in watching an old building come down. It is not, exactly, schadenfreude — the building has done no one any harm — but a more ambiguous emotion, in which one's interest in continuity is briefly overruled by a delight in the rare spectacle of irreversibility. We who spend our lives undoing minor errors, restoring drafts, and amending sentences are made strangely cheerful by an act that cannot be taken back, and the cheer outlasts our knowledge that we will, by tomorrow, have forgotten the building entirely.

question.question: What does the writer suggest is the deeper source of the pleasure of watching a demolition?
options: A) A genuine hostility toward the building, which had quietly offended the watcher in some indirect way
B) The rarity, for people whose lives are governed by revisable acts, of witnessing something genuinely irreversible
C) A nostalgic mourning for the building, made poignant by the certainty of its imminent and final disappearance
D) The visual interest of the spectacle, which provides ordinary entertainment without much further significance

78.description: C1–C2. 7 years. Qualification is essential to meaning. Sentences carry multiple subordinate clauses; each clause earns its place. Vocabulary around 17,800 words.

examples.passage: The distinction between persuasion and manipulation is harder to draw than most would-be ethicists allow. Persuasion, at its noblest, supplies reasons and trusts the listener to weigh them; manipulation bypasses that weighing process, working on appetites or fears below the threshold of conscious deliberation. But the line, in practice, is porous. A well-told story is more persuasive than the bare argument it dramatises, yet it functions partly through identification — through the kind of half-conscious sympathy that, in another context, we would call a manipulative appeal. To grant rhetoric its legitimate work is therefore to accept, uneasily, that the techniques we condemn in our opponents are the techniques we cannot quite abandon ourselves.

question.question: What is the writer's central observation?
options: A) Persuasion is always preferable to manipulation in serious public discourse
B) The boundary between them is blurry because effective persuasion borrows manipulative techniques
C) Modern audiences can no longer reliably distinguish between the two methods
D) Storytelling has replaced rational argument in nearly all forms of discourse

examples.passage: What is most striking about the rise of social media as a venue for political argument is not the coarsening of debate — that has been remarked upon to exhaustion — but the disappearance of the slow, intermediate form of reasoning that used to mediate between an initial reaction and a public utterance. Letters to the editor, even when intemperate, were written, set aside, and revised before posting. The friction was deliberate, even if no one called it that. Strip away that friction and you are left with a stream of first reactions, which is not the same thing as a public conversation, however much it superficially resembles one.

question.question: What does the writer identify as the most significant change in political discourse?
options: A) The growing coarseness and rudeness of public debate online
B) The removal of friction that once separated impulse from public statement
C) The replacement of newspapers with social media platforms
D) The increasing speed at which political news spreads across networks

79.description: C1–C2. 7 years. Long sentences with balanced constructions, embedded qualifications, and precise word choices. Vocabulary near 18,000 words.

examples.passage: To read Montaigne is to encounter a mind in motion — not the polished certainties of a moralist, but the provisional, self-correcting movements of someone genuinely thinking on the page. This is what makes his essays feel so contemporary: not their content, which is often antiquated, but their method, which is the method of someone who refuses to pretend he has finished thinking.

question.question: The author argues that Montaigne's essays feel contemporary despite often antiquated content. What makes this claim coherent rather than contradictory?
options: A) Modern readers find all historical writing relevant as long as it is written with elegance
B) The method of thinking-in-process outlasts its historical moment even when the subject matter does not
C) Montaigne's content is not actually antiquated — that description has been widely misapplied to him
D) Writers today consciously and deliberately set out to imitate Montaigne's distinctive style

examples.passage: Wittgenstein's later work has a strange effect on its readers. Those who arrive expecting a system, in the manner of his early Tractatus, are likely to come away convinced he had no system at all; those who arrive expecting nothing of the kind are equally likely to come away convinced that something tightly architectural is in fact at work, glimpsed only in the spaces between the numbered remarks. Both impressions are correct, which may be what he wanted.

question.question: What does the writer most plausibly take Wittgenstein's deliberate intention to have been?
options: A) To produce a fully systematic philosophy whose architectural structure is openly displayed for the reader's inspection
B) To leave readers with the consistent impression that no organizing scheme underlies the later work whatsoever
C) To make the question of whether his work has a system itself part of what readers must wrestle with
D) To repudiate the systematic ambitions of the Tractatus and replace them with a wholly fragmentary aphoristic style

80.description: C1–C2. 7–8 years. Demanding syntax; meaning sometimes arrives obliquely. Vocabulary around 18,500 words.

examples.passage: All her life she had confused being needed with being loved, and by the time she recognized the distinction it had already organized her most important relationships beyond easy revision. She did not blame anyone. That, too, she had learned late: that blame was just another way of remaining attached to something you could no longer change.

question.question: What does the character's refusal to blame anyone reveal about her understanding of attachment?
options: A) She is in denial about the harm that others have caused her over the years
B) She has seen that assigning blame would keep her connected to painful patterns rather than free her
C) She is emotionally unable to hold other people accountable for their actions toward her
D) She believes she alone is responsible for every difficulty in all her relationships

examples.passage: He had always assumed his father's silences were a kind of withholding — a refusal to give what he, as a son, had a right to expect. It was only after the funeral, sorting through letters his father had written to people he had never mentioned, that he understood the silences had not been withholding at all but a different kind of accuracy: the recognition that some feelings, when spoken, become smaller than they were before, and that his father had been protecting them, perhaps clumsily, by keeping them whole.

question.question: What revised understanding of his father does the son reach after the funeral?
options: A) The silences had been deliberate cruelties intended to deprive the son of paternal warmth he was owed
B) The silences had served to preserve feelings that the act of articulating them would have diminished
C) The father had loved other people more than his own son, as the unmentioned letters made plain to him
D) The father had been incapable of feeling anything at all, and the silences merely reflected that emotional void

81.description: C2 approach. 8 years. Complex periodic sentences with a strong authorial voice. The prose makes demands on patience and attention. Vocabulary near 19,000 words.

examples.passage: The argument that freedom of expression must be near-absolute rests on an epistemic claim that is often left unstated: that we cannot know in advance which ideas will prove valuable, and that the suppression of error has historically involved the suppression of truth with a frequency that should give us pause. This is a serious argument. It does not, however, settle the question of what to do about forms of speech whose primary function is not the communication of ideas but the intimidation of persons.

question.question: How does the author's final sentence complicate the epistemic argument for near-absolute free expression?
options: A) It concedes that the epistemic argument fails entirely and must simply be abandoned
B) It identifies a class of speech — intimidation rather than idea-communication — that falls outside the argument's reach
C) It argues that speech whose purpose is intimidation should be protected on epistemic grounds anyway
D) It shifts the entire debate away from philosophy and toward the domain of psychology

examples.passage: The case for global redistribution typically proceeds from one of two premises, which are often treated as interchangeable but which carry significantly different burdens of justification. The first is that the wealth of rich nations has been, in some morally salient sense, taken from poor ones, and that what is owed is therefore restitution rather than charity. The second is that, even setting historical injustice aside, current global inequality is sufficient on its own to generate strong duties of assistance. Defenders of redistribution who shift between these premises without notice make their position appear stronger than either premise, taken on its own, can support.

question.question: What is the writer's central methodological criticism of certain defenses of global redistribution?
options: A) The two premises are mutually contradictory, so any defense relying on either of them must necessarily collapse
B) Sliding between distinct premises lets a defense seem stronger than either premise can independently sustain
C) The historical-injustice premise is decisively false, which means defenses relying on it can be quickly dismissed
D) Current inequality is too modest to ground any genuine duties of assistance owed by the wealthy nations to the poor ones

82.description: C2. 8–9 years. High density of ideas per sentence. Allusions operate without signposting; considerable cultural literacy assumed. Vocabulary around 19,500 words.

examples.passage: The great nineteenth-century realist novel was, among other things, a training ground in the reading of social surfaces — in the interpretation of the significant detail, the telling gesture, the word that reveals more than its speaker intended. This is a skill that translates directly to life, which is perhaps why Middlemarch and Anna Karenina still feel, to their readers, less like historical documents than like mirrors.

question.question: Why, according to the author, do Middlemarch and Anna Karenina feel like 'mirrors' rather than 'historical documents'?
options: A) Both were written in a style that deliberately avoided period-specific historical detail
B) The skill of reading human behavior they develop in readers is as useful in the present as in the past
C) The central characters in both novels were closely based on real people readers can identify
D) The historical research behind both novels is so thorough that readers feel they are at real events

examples.passage: What distinguishes the late string quartets of Beethoven from his earlier work is not so much their technical demands, formidable as those are, as their structural impatience with the listener. The middle quartets reward attention with the satisfactions of an argument unfolding in time; the late quartets withdraw that contract, presenting figures and gestures that refuse to develop in the expected manner, that seem at moments to belong to no work at all but only to the silence that has briefly admitted them. To accuse them of formlessness is to confuse a different kind of form for the absence of one.

question.question: How does the writer answer the implied charge that Beethoven's late quartets are formless?
options: A) By conceding the charge and arguing the quartets remain valuable in spite of being formless
B) By treating the apparent formlessness as evidence of an unfamiliar form rather than the absence of form
C) By rejecting the comparison with the middle quartets, which the writer regards as significantly less mature
D) By arguing that the quartets do follow conventional forms when their structures are properly examined

83.description: C2. 9 years. Long sentences with multiple embedded clauses, precise and sometimes unusual vocabulary, a subtly ironic narrator. The prose rewards re-reading. Vocabulary near 20,000 words.

examples.passage: It was his habit, formed over decades of professional disappointment, to expect the worst from institutions while harboring an inexplicable tenderness for the individuals within them — a contradiction he had never resolved and had eventually decided to stop trying to resolve, on the grounds that most of the interesting things about a person are contradictions they have decided to stop resolving.

question.question: What does the character's reasoning for abandoning the attempt to resolve his contradiction reveal about his broader philosophy?
options: A) He believes any contradiction can be resolved if one simply applies enough sustained effort
B) He has concluded that an irresolvable contradiction is not a flaw but a feature of complex personhood
C) He is too intellectually lazy to examine his own inconsistencies with any real honesty
D) He learned from his professional life that institutions are irredeemably and universally corrupt

examples.passage: She had developed, somewhere in the course of her long professional silence, a manner of listening that was not, properly speaking, attentive — for the attentive listener still maintains a small reserve from which to formulate replies — but absorptive, as though the speaker's words entered some inner chamber from which they would, much later and in altered form, return. People who knew her well found this disconcerting, in the way that any disappearance of one's own remarks into a willing listener is disconcerting; and several of them, after a long enough acquaintance, came to depend on her precisely because of it.

question.question: What is the significance of the distinction the narrator draws between 'attentive' and 'absorptive' listening?
options: A) Attentive listening is a more polite social gesture, while absorptive listening fails to register anything that has been said
B) Attentive listening preserves a position from which to respond, while absorptive listening dissolves the listener's separateness
C) Absorptive listening is what trained therapists do, and the woman is therefore being characterized as a kind of clinician
D) Attentive listening produces sympathy, while absorptive listening produces hostility in the speaker who is being listened to

question.question: What does the woman's final decision not to have her question answered most precisely reveal about her predicament?

B) She has decided that her relationship with him has become so superficial in its mutual understanding that no question about its real nature could possibly produce an answer worth attending to, and she has therefore lost interest in the question itself

C) She has concluded that he genuinely does understand her in a way that is particular to her and not generalizable to any other woman, and the question has therefore become merely rhetorical and decorative for both of them

D) She has decided that she would rather direct the question to a third party who knows them both than rely on his own answer, since his answer would be too self-interested to settle the matter for her in the end
